sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Our Bordeaux data is recent; the figures below are for weekdays in August and September 2026. The Métropole's own reports supply the trend. Hourly use of METPARK's city-centre car parks fell 2% in 2024 and 3% in 2025, and is down 37% over several years, while subscribers fell too and public transport validations rose 9% and 3% [15][16]. Over five years the pedestrian area grew from 172 to 259 hectares, and footfall on the central shopping streets in December 2024 was 15% higher than a year earlier [17]. Fewer drivers use the central car parks, while footfall on the shopping streets has risen.

The city has used pricing more than prohibition. From May 2025 heavier cars were to pay 30% more on the street [10]. In August 2026 the old red and green zones became a single paid zone, billed by the half hour with 30 free minutes a day, up to €20 for four hours [11]. At the same time six METPARK car parks on the edge of the centre began offering two free hours at weekends [12]. Residents still pay little, €15 a month [13]. The low-emission zone was due to start in January 2025 with a narrow scope, banning only cars without a Crit'Air rating, about 2% of the local fleet, and keeping eleven park-and-ride sites open to them [8]. Nationally, an attempt to abolish such zones was struck down in May 2026 [9]. The park-and-ride fare is planned to rise from €4.50 to €5 in 2027 [14].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The Métropole is taking its car parks into its own hands. METPARK, its own parking authority, set up in 2004, runs about thirty car parks [0]; in 2023 the Métropole's car parks had 16,384 spaces, about three-quarters of them run by METPARK and the rest under concessions [1]. When the Camille Jullian concession held by Indigo ends in September 2026, METPARK is due to take it over, as approved in principle [5]. Ageing structures are a problem: the Front du Médoc car park has been closed since November 2023 after corroded beams were found [2]. The Gambetta car park reopened in November 2024 after renovation, with ticketless entry by number plate, real-time guidance signs and 102 spaces with charging [3][4].

Charging is moving into car parks on a large scale. TotalEnergies holds a 15-year concession for 1,500 charge points across 26 METPARK car parks [6], and by 2025 car parks held 958 publicly accessible charge points, a third of the area's total [7].

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
METPARK dominates. Its car parks typically charge €3–3.20 an hour and €23–24 a day, and price has no visible link with occupancy. They are well used, averaging 51–63% on weekdays. Q-Park has two car parks priced well above their neighbours, at 38%. Indigo and Effia hold a few sites, and the park-and-ride sites are run with the TBM transit network.

The fullest car parks form a ring just outside the historic core: Cité Mondiale (87%), Pey Berland (71%), Gambetta (73%) and, a little further out, Amplitude (74%). The garages within 500 m of the Place de la Comédie are quieter (36%); Camille Jullian stands at 12% just before its handover. The station car parks are commuter car parks, at 67% on weekdays and 32% at weekends. Park-and-ride use is uneven: Stalingrad, close to the centre, runs at 68%, while Les Aubiers and Quarante Journaux on the edge are almost empty (4–9%). The Mériadeck shopping centre's car park sits at 28%.
